claims.claim_text: KiCad dates from the mid-1990s, and its trajectory is the one common to long-lived open-source projects: little visible movement for many years followed by a period where capability accumulates faster than users can track.
claims.quote_verbatim: started in 96
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: A research laboratory assigning paid staff to work on the project changed its development rate, adding development capacity that a volunteer project cannot schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: this large lab is basically dedicating people to improving the software even faster
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: An open-source design tool needs a single project lead with a coherent direction rather than a committee pulling in different directions; the project acquired one who was employed full time to lead and co-develop it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it needs to come down to one person driving this thing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: For years the project expected users who wanted current features to compile the tool themselves, and per-platform builds were maintained by individual volunteers rather than by the project, with different people covering the Linux, Windows and macOS packages.
claims.quote_verbatim: the feeling is that if you want to be on the bleeding edge of KiCad, that you're going to compile it yourself
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: The project's position was that designating some builds as stable implies the others are not, so formal stable releases were avoided. The consequence for users is that a design tool, where stability matters more than features, offers no version the project itself recommends.
claims.quote_verbatim: they would much rather say every single release we make is stable
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: Working from nightly builds is less hazardous than it sounds: opening a nightly to find it unusable happened about five times in a year for one maintainer, whose practice was to update roughly fortnightly rather than daily.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would say it's probably happened five times this year
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: Anyone producing tutorial material against a fast-moving tool becomes pinned to an old version, because every interface change invalidates existing recordings; the alternative is maintaining a parallel track of the same course in the current version.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm still locked back in the past
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: The version 6 file format change is one-way: a project opened and saved in the new version cannot be returned to the old one, so upgrading is a decision about the whole project rather than a per-session choice.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you upgrade, you can't downgrade your files
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The project's original domain was registered personally by an early contributor rather than by any foundation, and when it was sold the project had to move to a new domain without a redirect, leaving stale links inside the application itself pointing at an address it no longer controlled.
claims.quote_verbatim: KeyCAD.org is the official new home of it

claims.claim_text: The abandoned original domain was subsequently cloned to look identical to the official site, with the instructions for verifying the downloaded package's hash removed. A design tool distributed by download is a supply-chain target, and the verification step is the defence that was deliberately taken away.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've removed how to validate that the package is correct

claims.claim_text: The project files are plain text, so they can be edited directly, diffed and placed under version control with ordinary tooling.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the files are textual you can edit them you can version control them
claims.speaker: Petr Dvorak
claims.episode_title: Freelance PCB Design with Petr Dvorak

claims.claim_text: What made version control and collaborative workflows work in software was that source is text, which anyone can build tools to process. Hardware's equivalent files are usually large, binary and proprietary, and that friction, not any difference in the work, is what has held equivalent hardware workflows back.
claims.quote_verbatim: our source files, so to speak, are CAD and they're binary and they're very large and they're proprietary
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Text files make export straightforward and import hard in the other direction: reading another vendor's binary format is where the difficulty lies, which is why importers for commercial formats are a continuing engineering effort rather than a solved problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's pretty easy to go from KiCad to something else because it's all ASCII

claims.claim_text: Because the design is text under version control, a repository hook fired by tagging a revision can regenerate the entire manufacturing package — Gerbers, schematic PDF and bill of materials — so that releasing a board becomes an act of tagging rather than a manual export sequence.
claims.quote_verbatim: It auto generates Gerbers. It regenerates a schematic file. It regenerates the bomb
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Such automation was for some time limited by the scripting interface rather than by the file format, since not every output step was reachable from a script.
claims.quote_verbatim: the API is catching up in terms of like scripting

claims.claim_text: The standard flow is a sequence of separate programs: draw the schematic, associate each schematic symbol with a footprint, import the resulting netlist and footprints into the layout tool, place, route, and plot the manufacturing files.
claims.quote_verbatim: you start out by making a schematic. Then once you make your schematic, you export that into the next
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: Tools differ in when the package decision is forced. Where a schematic symbol carries its footprint, the choice is made at part selection; where symbol and footprint are associated at the point of layout, the designer becomes the librarian for every part that lacks a ready footprint. Professional-tier tools tend to require correct library data up front on the assumption that a separate librarian produces it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're actually just putting in the schematic symbol. And then at the time when you're pulling it into the layout side, you actually, that's when you assign the, the package type
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: The gap between having chosen the components and being able to draw the schematic is filled by creating symbols and footprints, a task measured in weeks on a new design and repeated by every engineer using a different tool for the same part.
claims.quote_verbatim: you sit there for the next two weeks, getting all your symbols and your footprints in order
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Shared library efforts fail on insufficient structure rather than insufficient content. A manufacturer's downloadable library of a hundred symbols and footprints, five years old, takes longer to search and validate than creating the one part needed from the datasheet.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've not enforced enough structure onto the library
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Third-party libraries are installed by downloading files and placing them in the right location by hand rather than through the application, which is a barrier to using vendor-supplied parts even where they exist.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was hard to install. It wasn't easy to install that library
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The official library is maintained in a public repository by designated librarians and bundled with the installer; other vendors' libraries remain separate downloads.
claims.quote_verbatim: the latest build pulls, pulls in the, the GitHub controlled official KiCAD library

claims.claim_text: Footprints have long been atomic files, but a downloaded symbol arrived as a whole symbol library rather than a single part, so accumulating parts one at a time produced a library file per part. Version 6 makes symbols atomic in the same way, which fits the per-part download model that component library services use.
claims.quote_verbatim: the symbol is actually importing a, what it, what KiCAD interprets as a entire library
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Converting footprints between design tools is limited by what each format can express: slotted holes have no native representation in some tools and must be emulated on a milling layer, and support for them arrived comparatively late in others.
claims.quote_verbatim: in some cases there's, there's actually no way to create slotted holes in some PCB design tools
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Version 7 added a database-backed library, so a company can hold its parts in a database with multiple contributors and a librarian rather than in per-part files, which is the infrastructure a team rather than an individual needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can actually build a part database for yourself now instead of like doing it through individual files

claims.claim_text: A community script converts a distributor's part identifier directly into a local library entry, fetching symbol, footprint and 3D model in one command. The convenience trades against the discipline of maintaining a curated library, which remains the sounder practice.
claims.quote_verbatim: it grabs the footprint, it grabs the schematic, it grabs the 3d model, puts them all in a common library

claims.claim_text: Designs built around one assembler's in-house parts library get the smoothest and cheapest quotation, but the parts available in that library change, so the bill of materials must be reworked for each build rather than reused.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have to redo the bomb basically each and every time

claims.claim_text: The cost of a company changing design tools is dominated by recreating library data rather than by licences or retraining, which is why the switch is expensive even when the destination tool is free.
claims.quote_verbatim: redoing libraries, redoing this, redoing that. And it's like, that's when it gets really expensive

claims.claim_text: Inside companies nobody is rewarded for evaluating design tools, and the switching cost is already sunk into the incumbent, so a better tool does not displace it on merit. An open-source tool's route in is from the bottom, by being good enough that individuals bring it with them.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no incentive and nobody's encouraging you to, to, uh, to try new things and new tools
claims.speaker: Saar Drimer

claims.claim_text: Push-and-shove routing moves neighbouring traces out of the way while maintaining design rule clearances as the trace is dragged, so rule compliance is continuous rather than checked after the fact.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can drag your traces around and it keeps the, it keeps the design rules intact in real time
claims.speaker: Ben Krasnow
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow, 8 years on

claims.claim_text: The tool offers more than one rendering canvas, and the newer accelerated canvas handles operations such as reshaping a plane outline that are awkward in the default one; the choice of canvas therefore changes which editing operations are practical, not only how the board looks.
claims.quote_verbatim: polygons are a big problem in KiCad

claims.claim_text: Plane layers are plotted as positive images, unlike tools that treat plane layers as a distinct type plotted as negatives. The distinction matters at the fab, and the same board drawn with flooded signal layers instead of dedicated plane layers avoids the issue in either tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: it generates positive, uh, images, right? Even for planes
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Panelisation is not built in and is done by hand or by external scripts, which is a routine requirement for anyone having boards assembled rather than merely fabricated.
claims.quote_verbatim: KiCad doesn't have a panelization tool
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The tool's drawing origin sits at the top left while the assembly industry works from the bottom left corner of the board, so pick-and-place files carry coordinates in an unexpected frame; telling an assembler where zero is becomes a recurring source of confusion, and writing a parser for the format begins with resolving it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I still cannot figure out origins in ChiCAD
claims.speaker: Parker Dillman

claims.claim_text: Generating a usable placement file means setting the drawing origin deliberately to match the offset the machine expects, and converting the exported position file into the machine's own format, since the exported format is generic rather than machine-specific.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to set the origin in KiCad to match what that offset is going to be to the first component
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: One workable convention is to place the origin at the centre of the first component so every placement coordinate is measured from it, leaving the machine to relate that origin to the board's fiducials.
claims.quote_verbatim: the center of C1, which is my first component, is zero, zero

claims.claim_text: Length matching across a wide bus was done by assigning the signals to a custom net class and running a script that printed every net's length, then adding serpentine sections by hand until they agreed: a semi-automated loop built from the net class mechanism rather than a length-tuning feature.
claims.quote_verbatim: he defined custom net classes
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: Net classes are also where much of the design rule checking is configured, so grouping nets for one purpose changes the clearances applied to them.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's actually where a lot of the DRC stuff comes from as well
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: Matching physical lengths is not the same as matching propagation delay: signals routed on an inner layer travel at a different velocity from those on an outer layer, so a bus split across layers needs delay matching, which the length-matching tool does not provide and which was done in a spreadsheet alongside it.
claims.quote_verbatim: KeyCAD has length matching, but when you're routing a high-speed interface like this, you actually want delay matching
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Choosing a fabricator's published six-layer stack-up and routing on the outer layers gave a microstrip close to 50 ohms against a 40 ohm DDR3 target, close enough for a single memory device; moving those traces to an inner layer changes both impedance and propagation delay.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get a pretty nice microstrip that gets you somewhere close to 50 ohms
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Version 6 made design rules individually specifiable and scriptable, closing the gap with commercial tools where rules can be written per net, per area or per condition rather than applied globally.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the lacking in the V5 was kind of the, the individual nature of DRC

claims.claim_text: Electrical rule checking in schematic tools remains limited to pin types and voltage levels; checking that an I2C bus is connected to pins configured for I2C, on parts whose pin functions are set by internal multiplexers, is the class of error that current checking does not catch.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would actually like to do real, um, checking that you've got like analog signals connected to analog pins
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: A simulator is built into the schematic editor, so a captured schematic can be simulated without exporting to a separate package.
claims.quote_verbatim: ng-spice is now built into KiCad
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The board and its components can be exported as a STEP model for mechanical CAD, which is what makes fitting a board into an enclosure a mechanical rather than a guessing exercise.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kaikad actually has an option now for exporting, uh, step models
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: The exported 3D model carries only a plain board solid without copper or silkscreen, so producing a realistic render requires plotting the copper layers to SVG, converting them to an image and applying that as a texture to the solid in the mechanical tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: doesn't export the actual copper layers or the silkscreen
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: Switching to the three-dimensional view exposes mechanical conflicts, such as a button placed where a connector prevents it being pressed, that are invisible in the two-dimensional layout the designer has been staring at.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I switch into the 3d mode and I'm looking at the 3d board, suddenly I get so much more insight
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: Hiding the substrate in the 3D viewer and looking only at the vias and tracks is an effective way to build the mental model of how a multi-layer board connects, which is the step beginners find hardest when moving from lines on a screen to a physical stack-up.
claims.quote_verbatim: the 3d viewer is actually to turn off the FR4 visualization and just look at the vias

claims.claim_text: Direct mesh export, along with community add-ons that import a project with its 3D models intact, makes photorealistic rendering of a board possible without a commercial mechanical package in the path.
claims.quote_verbatim: key CAD is one of the only tools out there that would export directly to Blender as a mesh file
claims.speaker: Sam Aldhaher
claims.episode_title: Making The Invisible, Visible with Sam Aldhaher

claims.claim_text: A scalable bitmap can be placed in the layout as a tracing template, which is how an existing board with no surviving design files is recreated: the image is imported and the connections traced over it.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like scalable bitmaps that you can pull into the layout

claims.claim_text: Converting a bitmap into silkscreen artwork is handled by a conversion utility rather than being native to the editor, an approach shared with other tools where the same job is done by a long-lived script documented in the vendor's help pages.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a button in KiCad, but really I think that's just calling a script
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: Hatched copper fills are not supported, and the workaround is to place a repeated keepout or copper shape on a grid and let the fill flow around it. The technique is needed for capacitive touch designs, where a hatched plane lowers the plane's capacitance so it does not swamp the finger capacitance being measured, while still providing shielding.
claims.quote_verbatim: it looks like it doesn't exist currently

claims.claim_text: A Python scripting engine in the layout tool is what allowed community plugins to appear, including converters that turn the generic placement export into the format a particular pick-and-place machine expects.
claims.quote_verbatim: So now KiCad has a Python scripting engine
claims.episode_title: 3D Printed Shark Jumps - Edifying Edison's Energy

claims.claim_text: An open format plus a scripting interface lets third parties add tooling on top without the tool vendor's participation, and that layer of community tooling has produced capability that the core project did not have to build.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ability for someone to change KiCad and do like a tool that I can use and modify files is pretty trivial in Python

claims.claim_text: A shared-panel prototype service that began with almost all boards arriving in Eagle format saw KiCad rise to about 75 percent of submissions, with Eagle falling to a quarter or less; as professional firms began using the same service, commercial tools reappeared in the mix.
claims.quote_verbatim: is ended up being like 75% for, for a long time
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Download statistics from a cross-tool component library service put Altium at roughly 30 percent, Eagle at about 25 percent, and KiCad, OrCAD and Allegro at roughly 15 percent each, with the remainder spread across smaller tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium is probably like 30%. Eagle is probably like 25%
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Uptake in Asia has been low relative to the rest of the market, which matters because tooling and ecosystem support follow the installed base.
claims.quote_verbatim: keycads actually had really low uptake in asia

claims.claim_text: The decision to move an open-source hardware project off Eagle came when the design needed four layers: rather than pay to raise the licence tier, the project moved to a tool that anyone receiving the design could use to modify it. The same tool was subsequently used for designs involving FPGAs and USB 3.0.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't want people to have to pay for a license for some software to modify my open source design
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: The practical value of the tool being open source, for a user who does not contribute to it, is the option of fixing a blocking defect rather than waiting for a vendor; knowing the option exists changes the risk calculation of adopting it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I could, you know, I could dive in and, and work on it
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: Long-term access to a design is a licensing question rather than a technical one: an open tool can be preserved in a virtual machine and will still open the files decades later, with no licence server or expiry in the path.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can always have an old virtual machine running key cat five and 30 years from now, I will still be able to edit my designs
claims.speaker: Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: A competitor's move to subscription licensing was the trigger for experienced users to evaluate the open-source alternative, a pattern repeated across the professional user base rather than an isolated case.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was actually when they went to the subscription model that I decided to give KiCad a look
claims.speaker: Ben Krasnow
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow, 8 years on

claims.claim_text: There is no layer-count restriction of the kind free tiers of commercial tools have imposed, and high-speed differential pairs and arbitrary-angle routing are supported, so for the majority of professional work the tool rather than the licence is not the limiting factor.
claims.quote_verbatim: The number of layers in KCAD is like unlimited
claims.speaker: Petr Dvorak
claims.episode_title: Freelance PCB Design with Petr Dvorak

claims.claim_text: The identified limits are at the extremes: very high-density interconnect and very high-frequency designs, where the integrated simulation and interactive design assistance that commercial tools provide are absent. One consultant drew his own line at around twelve layers.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are missing simulations and online helpers as in Altium or PADS
claims.speaker: Petr Dvorak
claims.episode_title: Freelance PCB Design with Petr Dvorak

claims.claim_text: Capability and efficiency are separate questions: any board that can be designed at all can be designed in the tool, and the argument for a commercial package is the time it saves on a design that occupies a layout engineer for a month, not something it makes possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: I guarantee you can do any complexity board possible with KiCat
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Reusing a designed and laid-out block across projects is weak, which matters for consultancies that would otherwise carry a library of proven subcircuits from job to job.
claims.quote_verbatim: a key cad is actually terrible at a reusable block
claims.speaker: Scott Williams
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Because there is no vendor, there is no established route for a user to submit a feature request, which is a real cost of the model rather than an oversight. Version 5 brought the tool into line with standard interface conventions, including copy and paste of symbols.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not a commercial product. So there's not a really great channel for putting in feature requests
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Creating symbols for large components that must be split across multiple units has been a recurring source of defects, and library work generally is where users coming from commercial tools report the sharpest difference.
claims.quote_verbatim: especially when I created a new component footprint or symbol, actually symbols, if they're divided over multiple pages
claims.speaker: Shrouk El-Attar

claims.claim_text: Where a factory's engineers cannot open the design files, review can still be iterative: printing the board to PDF for annotation by hand and making the changes in the design tool keeps control of the design with its author rather than handing it to the factory.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was printing out PDFs of the board, and their EE was drawing on them

claims.claim_text: A supply chain that cannot read the design files at all is a constraint on tool choice, since the interchange format becomes whatever both sides can process.
claims.quote_verbatim: their EE couldn't open Gerber's

claims.claim_text: An entrant tool can serve manufacturing only because the industry's interchange formats are standardised and open. Where the handoff runs on Gerbers and spreadsheets, the design tool at the other end is irrelevant to the assembler.
claims.quote_verbatim: spreadsheets and Gerbers are the only reason that Kaikad can, you know, operate in that space
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Rapid feature addition is simultaneously the project's advantage and its cost to institutional users, who value a tool that does not change between projects; the interface changes are where users notice it most.
claims.quote_verbatim: how fast, uh, new features get added to it
claims.speaker: Stephen Craig

claims.claim_text: Moving between layout tools is largely a matter of relearning where the commands are, since the underlying flow of placing symbols, defining pins and connecting them is common; the transferable skill is the flow, not the tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: Jumping to KiCad, not that hard because I understood the basic flow
claims.speaker: Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: Import of the competing hobbyist format, including its libraries, became reliable in version 5, removing the need to redraw an existing body of work in order to move.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the Eagle import. To Kaikad is now. In five. Is like solid

claims.claim_text: Importers for commercial formats are treated as strategically necessary rather than optional, on the reasoning that a tool nobody can move their existing projects into cannot displace an incumbent.
claims.quote_verbatim: the importer for Altium files has gotten better

claims.claim_text: An earlier approach went further than conversion, reading another tool's libraries directly with no import step, gated behind a compile-time switch while it was experimental.
claims.quote_verbatim: it will let you open up an Eagle, an Eagle library and use those parts without any sort of import process
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: A contemporary open-source layout tool was arguably ahead technically in the early years; the outcome was decided by which project accumulated contributors and support rather than by the initial capability of either.
claims.quote_verbatim: it probably would have been better than key cared back in the day
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Data Provenance in the Home, Server, and Fab

claims.claim_text: A tool with no licence cost can be introduced two years earlier in an engineering curriculum than one requiring seats, which changes what students can be asked to do and what they can demonstrate outside the course.
claims.quote_verbatim: I use key CAD for electronic schematic capture in the sophomore level class and spice simulation
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: Running the tool on identical single-board computers with pre-imaged storage removes the first hours of an in-person course, which are otherwise spent installing drivers and software on a room of dissimilar laptops.
claims.quote_verbatim: KaiCat works A-OK on Raspberry Pi
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade

claims.claim_text: Platform coverage has been uneven, with the macOS build long unusable enough that presenting the tool meant running it in a virtual machine on another operating system.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is no stable build for Mac at all
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: An open tool does not displace incumbents by matching them feature for feature; it does so by being distinctly good at enough of the work to be brought in from below, where no procurement decision is required.
claims.quote_verbatim: it doesn't have to be awesome in all respects, but it can be something that is really, really good
claims.speaker: Saar Drimer
